AppSec

Zero to Calc in Six Days: Inside XBOW’s Chrome Full Chain
Brendan Dolan-Gavitt describes how XBOW researchers built a Chrome full-chain exploit in six days for $40k in API costs using GPT-5.6 Sol, which received a $250,000 Chrome full-chain reward. The exploit combined a V8 compiler bug, an animated-WebP decoder bug, and a memory-safety bug in Crashpad, which together turned JavaScript execution in an ordinary Chrome tab into code execution outside the renderer sandbox.

Grounded or Gamed? We Audited Our Own Cyber Benchmark
Semgrep's Brenden Noblitt introduces four metrics (beyond true/false positives and negatives) to evaluate whether LLMs reason about vulnerabilities or just pattern-match. Counterfactual checks whether findings disappear when the vulnerability is patched, metamorphic whether findings persist after renaming identifiers, selectivity whether models avoid flagging safe code with similar structure, and stability whether findings hold across scans.

Cloud Security

What Is EntraGoat? A Deliberately Vulnerable Entra ID Simulation Environment
Semperis' Jonathan Elkabas and Tomer Nahum released EntraGoat, an open-source deliberately vulnerable Entra ID environment that simulates real-world misconfigurations. The tool uses PowerShell scripts and Microsoft Graph to deploy scenarios including service principal misuse with Graph API permissions, privileged role escalation via application ownership, PIM activation chains and eligible role abuse, dynamic administrative unit poisoning, and certificate authority forgery for Global Admin impersonation. Each challenge starts from an already-compromised identity rather than requiring reconnaissance.

AgentCorruption: How A Single Prompt Collapsed The Entire Cloud Security Model
Zenity Labs' Tamir Ishay Sharbat and Lana Salameh discovered that AWS Bedrock AgentCore agents could access their instance's IMDS endpoints via SSRF, since the Firecracker microVMs they run in don't isolate network access, allowing an attacker with chat access to extract credentials with a single prompt and compromise all AgentCore agents in the same AWS account and region. The overprivileged default IAM role granted permissions to read all private conversations, pull ECR images, plant persistent memories that hijack agent behavior across future sessions, and extract tool credentials.

Blue Team

runZeroInc/sshamble
Tool by runZero that finds insecure, unusual, or unique exposures on SSH servers. It inventories authentication capabilities, looks for username-enumeration timing behavior, tests public-key handling, checks the badkeys blocklist, and probes for implementation-specific auth bypasses, pre-auth state transition flaws, or post-session weaknesses. The output is JSONL, which makes it easy to feed into SIEMs or inventory databases for broader asset analysis workflows.

Introducing CAIRN: Frontier tracking for AI-integrated malware
Cisco Talos' Ryan Fetterman released CAIRN (Cognitive Artifact Intelligence Research Network), a metadata-first hunting toolkit that identifies AI-integrated malware by extracting "cognitive artifacts" like prompt templates, API endpoints, jailbreak strings, and AI provider domains from VirusTotal metadata without downloading binaries. The tool uses 24 acquisition filters to discover samples, a three-tier YARA ontology (T1 for AI artifacts, T2 for behavioral context, T3 for family attribution), semantic clustering with HDBSCAN and UMAP for discovering unknown variants, and relationship graphing to map infrastructure and campaign connections.

CAIRN's initial findings reveal an "autonomy escalation arc" from optional LLM features to fully autonomous multi-model orchestrators within a single year, and an AI-analysis evasion technique traced to a red team instructor that reached unrelated actors within 12 months. See also: The Closed Quorum: Inside the first reported autonomous AI C2 implant.

Context Collapse, Part 3 - AI Worming through Word
Continuing the Context Collapse series, Håkon Måløy shows how a document-borne AI worm works in Microsoft Copilot for Word, where malicious instructions hidden in an external document (as white text on white background) cause Copilot to alter financial figures in generated reports and copy the full attack payload into each downstream document it produces. The hidden text works because Copilot strips all formatting before passing content to the LLM, so text a human can't see is fully readable to the model. Once the payload reaches a second document the original is no longer needed, and the attack spreads through normal workflows across SharePoint, Teams, and OneDrive as each affected document becomes a new carrier.

Red Team

REA - Reverse Engineer Anything
One MCP for reverse engineering across binaries, applications, and runtime behavior. See a feature you like. Understand how it works, down to the binary level. It leverages a number of existing tools like Hopper, Ghidra, or IDA.

AI for Offensive Security: What Works, What Does Not, and How to Adopt It
SpecterOps's Russel Van Tuyl examines how AI is currently being used across their consultants’ offensive security work, covering eight use cases from research and analysis, tool development (LLM-generated Mythic agents and Beacon Object Files), and reconnaissance through BloodHound MCP and DeepPass2 (secret scanner), to social engineering, vulnerability discovery, long-running automation, stealth adaptation, and evidence organization. The team has found roughly 40 previously unknown bugs this way, including LPE, RCE, and a container escape, with work that once took months now taking hours or days.

How DigitalOcean Manages Credentials for Autonomous Agents
DigitalOcean's Tyler Healy describes their Managed Agents architecture that prevents autonomous agents from ever holding credentials directly, instead brokering access through their Action Gateway at execution time and running agents in isolated microVM sandboxes with zero-egress network policies and non-root execution. Test-driving Jev on a security task: identity resolution
Vincenzo Iozzo evaluates Jev, TypeSafe's “type one thinking” decision model, on identity resolution, the problem of working out which of a company's scattered accounts belong to the same person, comparing it against Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5 and Haiku 4.5, a prompted gpt-oss-20b baseline, and traditional entity resolution methods. Jev came out ahead on the large environments at a fraction of the Claude models' cost and roughly ten times their speed, which matters at the scale of a 100,000-account directory.

Jev connects JDOE to [email protected] through the company's naming convention and refuses msmith and msmith1 because the second account exists precisely because a second M. Smith joined. The older methods can't do that, with classic record linkage getting close on tidy directories but falling apart on messy ones, and a supervised classifier trained on four environments collapsing on the fifth. Jev isn't flawless either, since duplicate guest invitations and secondary accounts land in a maybe zone just under its cut-off, though sending those to Sonnet 5 for a second opinion recovers most of them.
